title: RESTful API Design Principles
description: Learn the core principles behind RESTful APIs, including statelessness, resource orientation, and uniform interface constraints that make APIs scalable and maintainable.

data.text: REST, or Representational State Transfer, is an architectural style for designing networked applications. It relies on a stateless, client-server communication model where requests are made over HTTP. In a RESTful API, everything is treated as a resource, and each resource is identified by a unique URI. Understanding REST principles helps you design APIs that are predictable, scalable, and easy to consume. When you design with REST in mind, clients interact with resources in a consistent way regardless of the underlying implementation.

REST is built on six constraints. Client-server separation allows each side to evolve independently. Statelessness means every request contains all information needed to process it, with no session state stored on the server. Cacheability lets responses be marked as cacheable or non-cacheable, improving performance. Uniform interface simplifies the architecture by decoupling implementation from the interface. Layered system allows intermediaries like load balancers and proxies. Code-on-demand is the only optional constraint, allowing servers to extend client functionality. Together, these constraints create an environment where systems can grow without friction.

data.title: Why Statelessness Matters
data.text: Stateless APIs scale horizontally because any server can handle any request. This eliminates sticky sessions and makes load balancing straightforward, which is why cloud-native systems almost always favor stateless designs.

In REST, nouns represent resources rather than verbs representing actions. A resource can be a user, order, product, or any entity in your domain. Each resource is accessed through a URI such as /users or /orders/123. The API uses standard HTTP methods to perform operations on those resources, keeping the interface intuitive and consistent. This mapping between domain concepts and URLs is what makes REST easy to learn and document.

data.title: Resource-Oriented Endpoints
data.content: Instead of exposing action-based URLs, map your domain to resources.
data.code:
GET    /users/42          → Retrieve user 42
POST   /users             → Create a new user
PUT    /users/42          → Replace user 42
PATCH  /users/42          → Update user 42
DELETE /users/42          → Delete user 42

data.text: A uniform interface is the heart of REST. It consists of four key elements. Resource identification in requests uses URIs to name each resource. Resource manipulation through representations lets clients modify data by exchanging JSON or XML documents. Self-descriptive messages include media types and metadata so servers know how to process them. Hypermedia as the engine of application state, often abbreviated HATEOAS, embeds links in responses so clients can discover available actions dynamically.

data.title: Elements of a uniform interface
items: Resource identification in requests using URIs.
Resource manipulation through representations such as JSON.
Self-descriptive messages with media types and HTTP methods.
Hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS), where responses include links to related actions.

items.question: Is REST the same as HTTP?
items.answer: No. REST is an architectural style, while HTTP is a protocol that can implement RESTful constraints. You can have REST over other protocols, but HTTP is the most common choice.

items.question: Does REST require JSON?
items.answer: No. REST supports any representation format including XML, HTML, or plain text. JSON is widely used because it is lightweight and easy to parse in JavaScript clients.

data.title: Takeaway
points: REST relies on stateless, resource-oriented design.
Uniform interface reduces coupling between client and server.
Cacheability and layered systems improve performance and scalability.
data.takeaway: Mastering REST principles helps you design APIs that are easy to use, easy to test, and easy to scale.
